readerTitle: The big order that could double the factory, or sink it
caseNote: 가상 사례 (플라스틱 운송 상자 제조 공장, B2B 예약 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: '빨리 성장할까, 수익을 지킬까'는 성격의 문제가 아니다. 성장이 나중에 무엇을 사 오는지 묻고, 나쁜 미래에서도 살아남도록 계획을 바꾸는 문제다.
misconception: 성장이 장기 전략이고 수익은 단기 전략이다. 큰 기회가 오면 잡는 쪽이 장기적으로 옳다.

sources.text: THK-09-01 단기·장기 트레이드오프, THK-09-04 시나리오 사고 (이 유닛의 개념 레슨)

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 공장 시나리오 계산: 신규 라인 $400,000, 주문의 연간 공헌이익 $180,000(연 매출 $1.2M 기준). 3년 유지: 180 × 3 = 540 − 400 = +$140k. 1년 후 이탈: 180 − 400 = −$220k. 2년차부터 10% 가격 인하: 인하액 $120k → 연 공헌이익 $60k, 180 + 60 + 60 = 300 − 400 = −$100k.
소프트웨어 사례는 수치 없이 일반 원리로만 서술했습니다. 특정 기업이나 업계 평균 이탈률 통계는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The big order that could double the factory, or sink it
body: Dana runs a 40-person plant that makes plastic shipping crates. It has been profitable for eight years, mostly selling to regional food distributors.

Then a national retailer calls. It wants a contract worth $1.2 million a year, nearly doubling her sales. To fill it, she needs a new production line. It costs $400,000, and she would have to borrow it.

image.label: A small factory floor with a huge order sheet arriving
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 작은 공장 안, 플라스틱 상자가 쌓인 생산 라인 옆에서 공장주가 바닥까지 늘어진 거대한 주문서를 들고 있음. 한쪽 벽에 빈 자리(새 라인이 들어갈 공간)가 점선으로 표시됨. 실제 유통사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Grow fast or stay profitable?
body: Dana's banker says the loan is easy to get. Her production manager is excited. Her accountant reminds her the plant has never had debt.
What should Dana do first?

options.text: Sign it. A national retailer could make the company
options.feedback: You'd gain scale, but you'd bet the plant on one future. Scenario thinking asks what happens if the retailer leaves after a year.

options.text: Say no. The plant is profitable and the order is risky
options.feedback: You protect this year's profit. But that is a short-term vs long-term trade-off too: you may give up scale that keeps you competitive later.

options.text: First sketch how the deal plays out if the retailer stays, leaves or cuts the price
options.feedback: This turns a gut call into a question you can answer: which futures can the plant survive? That's scenario thinking at work.

cards.eyebrow: Concept at work · Trade-offs over time
cards.title: The real choice is about time, not growth.
body: A **short-term vs long-term trade-off** means giving up something now to get something later, or the reverse. Fast growth usually spends today's profit to buy future scale, customers or position. Staying profitable keeps today's money but can cost tomorrow's position.
So "grow or stay profitable" is the wrong question. The useful one is: what exactly does the growth buy, and how sure is it to arrive?
For Dana, the order buys volume. Volume only pays off if it lasts long enough to repay the new line.

cards.title: Three futures for the same contract.
body: Assume the order leaves $180,000 a year after materials, labor and freight. The new line costs $400,000. Here is where Dana stands after three years in each future.

breakdown.label: Retailer cuts price 10% in year two
Retailer leaves after one year
breakdown.detail: Loan still due, line sits idle

cards.callout: The growth plan wins in one future and loses in two.

cards.title: Change the deal, not just the answer.
body: Scenario thinking doesn't stop at yes or no. It asks how to make the plan survive the bad futures.
Dana goes back with terms: a three-year minimum volume, a limit on price changes, and leasing the line instead of buying it. She also sets a rule that her old customers must stay above half of sales.
Now the growth bet doesn't need the best future to work. It only needs her to avoid the worst one.

image.label: Three paths, two with safety nets added
image.brief: 세 갈래 길 인포그래픽. "Stays", "Price cut", "Leaves" 세 길이 있고, 아래 두 길에 안전망이 새로 설치됨. 안전망 라벨: "3-year minimum", "Lease, don't buy", "Keep old customers". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Growth spending only works if customers stay.
body: A subscription software company faces the same choice. It can spend heavily on ads and sales, losing money each month, or grow slowly and stay profitable.
The long-term logic holds only if customers stay long enough to repay what it cost to win them. If many leave within a few months, the "long term" never arrives.
And there's a scenario to plan for: what if the next round of funding doesn't come?

cards.title: "Long term" can become an excuse.
body: Fast growth's payoff is a forecast. Today's profit is a fact. It's easy to call any loss an investment.
But staying profitable isn't automatically safe either. A rival who grows can win the big customers, lower its costs and set the price you have to match.
Neither path is the cautious one by default. The cautious path is the one you've tested against the futures that could hurt you.

cards.title: Now it's a scheduling software company.
body: You sell booking software to clinics and salons. You're slightly profitable and have cash for 18 months if you start losing money. A board member urges you to triple ad spending and hire sales staff to grab the market before rivals do.
What do you do?

options.text: Triple spending now. Market share is what lasts
options.feedback: You'd buy speed, but only the best future works. If funding dries up or customers churn, the cash runs out before growth pays back.

options.text: Stay profitable and keep spending flat
options.feedback: You avoid running out of cash, but this trades long-term position for short-term safety. Rivals may sign the customers you'd need later.

options.text: Raise spending in steps, keep a cash floor, and scale only if new customers keep paying
options.feedback: You still invest in the long term, but you've planned for the bad scenarios. Each step happens only if the payoff is actually showing up.

cards.title: Ask what growth buys, then plan for the futures that hurt.
body: Two ideas from this unit did the work in this lesson:
list: **Short-term vs long-term trade-offs:** name what growth costs now and what it should buy later
**Scenario thinking:** test the plan in good, bad and middle futures, then change it so you survive the bad ones
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take your next growth idea. Write what it costs, what it buys, and what happens if your key customer leaves in a year.
